results.title: How Long Does It Take to Open a Bank Account in Finland? - Finland Handbook
results.author: Finland Handbook Editorial Team
highlights:
## The Realistic Timeline for Opening a Finnish Bank Account

When you first arrive in Helsinki, Tampere, or any other Finnish city, you might expect to walk into a branch and leave with an active account twenty minutes later. Unfortunately, the reality for most expats is a bit more protracted. Depending on your residency status and the specific bank, the process can take anywhere from two weeks to two months. It is essential to understand that there is a difference between having a basic account and having the full suite of digital services that make life in Finland functional.

### The Appointment Waiting Game

The first hurdle is often just getting through the door. In many parts of Finland, banks like Nordea, OP (Osuuspankki), and Danske Bank have moved toward an appointment-only model for new customers. I remember sitting in a lobby for two hours only to be told that the next available slot for an "onboarding meeting" was three weeks away. This is a common scenario in larger cities where the influx of international workers and students is high.

Once you secure an appointment, the meeting itself is usually straightforward, lasting about 45 to 60 minutes. During this time, the bank will perform their Know Your Customer (KYC) checks. They will ask about the source of your funds, your expected monthly turnover, and whether you are a politically exposed person. While this feels intrusive, it is standard procedure under Finnish anti-money laundering laws. If you are prepared, this part of the journey is the fastest, but the lead time to get that seat in the office is what usually catches newcomers off guard.

...

After your meeting, the bank doesn't always flip a switch to activate your account. Your documents often need to be verified by a central back-office team. If you are an EU citizen with a valid passport and a Finnish personal identity code, this might happen in a few days. However, if you are from outside the EU and your residence permit is still being processed or if the bank needs to verify foreign employment contracts, you could be looking at a one-to-two-week wait just for the "approval" phase.

...

There is a frustrating nuance in Finnish banking called "Strong Identification" (vahva tunnistautuminen). This is the digital key that allows you to log into everything from the tax office to the healthcare portal. Even after your bank account is open and you have a debit card, the bank may wait an additional three months before granting you these digital credentials if you are a new resident.

...

The physical card and the PIN code for the card are usually mailed to your home address in two separate envelopes for security reasons. This usually takes 5 to 7 business days after the account is approved. However, the activation of the digital app—which you use for online shopping and ID verification—might require a second visit to the branch. Always ask during your first meeting: "Do I need to come back in person to activate the digital ID, or can I do it through the app once my card arrives?"

results.title: Opening a Bank Account in Finland as a Foreigner | NordicExpat
results.author: Bikram Nath
highlights:
How long

About 5–10 days from appointment at OP once you have your HETU and documents

...

Opening a bank account in Finland takes longer than in many countries, mostly for two reasons: traditional banks require a henkilötunnus (Finnish personal identity code — your national ID number) and an in-person identity check before they will open a standard account. Realistically, plan for the whole journey — from landing in Finland to having a working account with online codes — to take several weeks, because you also need to complete DVV registration first. A Finnish account is more than a place to park your salary, though: the online banking codes it gives you, the pankkitunnukset ("bank credentials"), double as your digital identity for almost every government and private service in the country. This guide covers what you need, which bank suits a newcomer, what the in-person visit involves, costs and timelines, the rights you have if you are refused, and what to use in the meantime.

...

### OP (Osuuspankki)

Finland's largest banking group by customer count — a cooperative with regional banks and branches nationwide. Well-suited to people settling for the long term.

- Requires a valid passport or national ID, proof of right of residence, and a Finnish address.
- States there is "no workaround" — the henkilötunnus is essential for opening an account and for full online banking.
- Identity is verified in person at a branch. Non-EU citizens may need extra steps (for example a Finnish ID card) to enable strong electronic identification.
- Describes a realistic timeline of roughly 5–10 days once documents are complete (verify on op.fi).

...

Even when you start an application online, all major Finnish banks require an in-person identity-verification visit for a first Finnish account — partly because, until you hold strong electronic identification, you cannot legally sign the documents online. At the branch:

1. Bring every required document — passport or EEA ID card, henkilötunnus, residence document, and proof of address.
2. Identity verification — a bank employee checks and copies your documents and confirms your identity in person.
3. Sign the agreements — you sign the account agreement and the related services agreement.
4. Wait for the post — account details, your debit card, and your online banking codes are typically mailed.

Book the appointment in advance — walk-in service for new account openings is not guaranteed, and at busy branches the wait for a slot can itself add days. For service in English, ask for it when you book; Nordea has a dedicated English line.

...

The ... of ... : ... carry a ... service ... ( ... 1 ... and ... within the ... and ... on ... and ... exactly ... service ... tends to beat a ... .

Timeline. OP describes a realistic 5–10 days from a complete application to a working account, with about a week being the fastest case. But that clock starts only once you have your henkilötunnus and documents — so the full journey from arrival is longer. A sensible mental model: DVV registration and identity code first (often the slowest step), then about a week for the bank, then 1–2 weeks for codes and card by post. Confirm timelines directly with DVV and your bank, as they shift with caseload.

...

You still need to receive your first salary and pay for things in that window.

...

How long does it take to open a Finnish bank account?

Once you have your henkilötunnus and documents in order, OP describes a realistic timeline of about 5–10 days, with roughly one week being the fastest if everything is complete (as of 2026 — check op.fi). Add the DVV registration and identity-code wait on top of that, so plan for the whole journey from arrival to take several weeks. Online banking codes and your card typically arrive by post after the branch visit.

results.title: Turkish citizen faces challenges opening bank account in Finland - Daily Northern
highlights:
Mehmet Hakan Bedestenlioğlu, a Turkish citizen, arrived in Finland about a month ago, as his wife began her master’s studies at the University of Jyväskylä. The family plans to stay in Finland for at least a few years. However, Bedestenlioğlu has faced significant challenges in opening a bank account, having tried at four different banks without success.

He expressed feelings of desperation, stating, “I feel hopeless because no one is helping me. Without a bank account, I can’t do anything.” Each bank presented unique obstacles: one required a Finnish identity card, another a Finnish-speaking assistant, one was unresponsive, and the last had no available appointments for the next month. Although Bedestenlioğlu speaks fluent English, Finnish banks are required to operate primarily in Finnish or Swedish.

...

When asked about their language policies, Osuuspankki, Nordea, and S-Pankki provided varied responses, with some offering services in English. Notably, S-Pankki mentioned that services are primarily in Finnish and Swedish, with limited English support. However, after this article was drafted, Bedestenlioğlu reported good news: he successfully opened a bank account in Finland.
